paras: The shooting of Mack Henry and his wife was an ambush in Florida on February 17, 1888, in which unknown parties fired buckshot at Henry, a one-armed Black man, at the door of his home, killing his wife and seriously wounding him. Henry survived, but a Lake City report in late July said he had been shot and killed by an unknown assassin at the same place.

Henry, described as "colored," had just served a year in the state penitentiary from Columbia county for stealing the hogs of Willie Sparkman of Suwanee county. According to the Savannah Morning News, he came home "enraged with his accusers, who were both white and colored," and threatened to take their lives.

On Friday, February 17, Henry came home from a ride, handed his horse to a boy, and as he tried to walk in his door "was shot down by unknown parties." His wife, who was sitting in the doorway, received part of the load meant for him and was killed instantly. Three buckshot struck Henry, who was seriously wounded but not killed.

No report of an inquest or arrest for the February shooting appears in the coverage. On July 31 the paper's Lake City correspondent wrote that Henry had been "shot and killed by some unknown assassin near Ichetuchnee Friday." The same letter said his wife had been killed "at the same place in the same clandestine manner" and that efforts were being made to apprehend the guilty party.

Both known reports ran in the Savannah Morning News, the first among routine notes in its Florida news column and the second at the end of a Lake City letter about other matters. The February item set out Henry's conviction and threats before the shooting, without comment, while the July letter spoke of an "unknown assassin"; neither named a motive.

The two reports differ on when Henry's wife was killed: the February item gives Friday, February 17, while the July letter says "about three months ago." The February report, printed ten days later with an exact date, is the closer source.

reader.title: Shooting of Mack Henry and his wife
bases: Both reports attribute the shootings to unseen 'unknown parties' or an 'unknown assassin' firing on Henry at his home, and neither describes a mob, band, posse or crowd (A1, A2).

The February news column describes the shooting that killed Henry's wife (A1), and a separate Lake City letter five months later independently says his wife was shot and killed in a clandestine manner at the place where Henry was later killed, though it dates her death 'about three months ago' (A2).

accounts.label: Florida news column (February)
accounts.gist: After returning from prison and threatening his accusers, Henry was shot down at his door by unknown parties; his wife was killed instantly and he was seriously wounded.

accounts.label: Lake City correspondent (July)
accounts.gist: Henry was shot and killed by an unknown assassin near Ichetuchnee; his wife had been shot and killed at the same place in the same clandestine manner about three months earlier.

framing.detail: The February item sets Henry's prison term and threats against his accusers before the shooting without comment, and names the shooters only as 'unknown parties'.
The July Lake City letter calls the killings 'clandestine' and notes efforts to apprehend 'the guilty party'.

versions.value: 'about three months ago' as of late July 1888 (around late April)

conflicts.note: The February report gives an exact date ten days after the event and is the better evidence for the date; the July figure is a correspondent's approximation.
